In 2025, about 96% of new cars sold in Norway were electric. Petrol and diesel are now a rounding error there.

One map, and a policy blueprint 30 years in the making — a thread 🧵🗺️

Data: Our World in Data (CC BY)

1/ The map shows the electric share of new car sales in 2025, battery and plug-in hybrid combined. Norway and its Nordic neighbors are the darkest green on Earth, with China close behind. Most of Africa and South Asia are blank — too few EVs to register.

2/ Norway's EV boom didn't start with Tesla. It started in 1990, when the country exempted electric cars from its steep purchase tax — funded, ironically, largely by revenue from Norway's own oil and gas industry.

3/ Through the 1990s and 2000s Norway kept stacking incentives: no VAT on EVs from 2001, free municipal parking, reduced tolls, bus-lane access, free ferry crossings. None of it was subtle, and it added up fast.

4/ Cheap, clean electricity mattered just as much. Norway generates almost all its power from hydropower, so charging an EV there has long been both cheap and low-carbon — an advantage few countries can simply copy.

5/ China's rise on the map runs on a different mechanism: industrial policy. Beijing subsidized EV and battery manufacturing for over a decade, built the world's largest charging network, and now sells more EVs domestically than almost any legacy automaker.

6/ The gap that remains is stark. The US sits in a much lighter band, and most of the Global South is uncolored entirely — EVs are still priced for wealthy, subsidy-backed markets, not the world's median car buyer.
